name: fIREHOSE
label: SST
lede: Mike Watt and George Hurley lost D. Boon in December 1985 and weren't planning a sequel. Then a 21-year-old from Ohio kept phoning, and by the end the three had played about 980 gigs.

eras.title: The kid who kept calling
eras.text: After D. Boon died, Mike Watt and George Hurley had no band and no plan for one. An Ohio college kid acting on a false rumor changed that, and within months the three were playing under a name lifted from a Bob Dylan film clip.

q: He kept calling me up, kept calling and calling.
years.h: A false rumor sends Ed Crawford to the phone
years.p: [[Ed Crawford|c02f03fe-93cf-4590-841b-1b9f04d6a694]], a 21-year-old Ohio State student, heard the Minutemen survivors were auditioning guitarists. They weren't. He got [[Mike Watt|568203ae-c27b-4990-8997-09c0d5c0de77]]'s number at a Columbus show and called anyway.
years.xp:
Crawford had come out of a Minutemen show saying he'd rarely been so moved by a live band. Watt, still grieving, kept saying no. Crawford flew to Southern California and kept asking to jam, and right before he was due back in Ohio, Watt gave in.

At the San Pedro tryout Crawford played [[The Who|9fdaa16b-a6c4-4831-b87c-bc9ca8ce7eaa]]'s I'm One and Minutemen songs, and Watt and [[George Hurley|e3644b83-1c19-41fa-bf81-483551cd1588]] asked him to join. Crawford told Jambands he had gone expecting feedback on his playing, and recalled Watt's reply: "When can you move out here?"

years.h: Nine months under Mike Watt's desk
years.p: Now 'ed fROMOHIO', Crawford sleeps under a desk in Watt's one-bedroom apartment in San Pedro for nine months.

years.h: Bob Dylan names the band; the lowercase f nods to Minutemen
years.p: The name comes from Bob Dylan's Subterranean Homesick Blues film clip. The small f answers the all-caps MINUTEMEN logo.

years.cap: fIREHOSE at Angels Gate Band Day, San Pedro, 1986, likely the first gig
years.h: Six months after Boon, Watt and Hurley are back onstage
years.p: The first fIREHOSE gig, in June 1986 in San Pedro, with Crawford on guitar.

years.h: Sonic Youth takes them out on the Flaming Telepaths Tour
years.p: [[Sonic Youth|5cbef01b-cc35-4f52-af7b-d0df0c4f61b9]] had pulled Watt out of his grief by putting him on EVOL. Now they bring fIREHOSE on the road.
Rockers like Choose Any Memory sit beside quiet pieces like The Candle and the Flame. Trouser Press called it "bracing" and heard integrity from start to finish.
years.xp:
Trouser Press said the LP "jumps all over the map, from edgy rockers to absorbing mood pieces to acoustic reveries." It honored Boon without imitating him.

The pro-shot broadcast of the Mississippi Nights show in St. Louis, from November 8, 1986, shows the line-up the record came out of.

eras.title: Records to promote tours
eras.text: The van came first and the albums followed. By the third record, fIREHOSE had worked country-rock and skate-video exposure into something that didn't sound like Minutemen or anyone else.

years.h: If'n hands Crawford the mic and parodies R.E.M.
years.p: Crawford sings lead on Anger, the band slips in a send-up of [[R.E.M.|ea4dfa26-f633-4da6-a52a-f49ea4897b58]], and Watt adds a spoken-word piece.
years.xp: Trouser Press heard a band with more confidence and more articulation, "unpredictable and unpretentious."

years.h: Watt marries Black Flag bassist Kira Roessler
years.p: [[Mike Watt|568203ae-c27b-4990-8997-09c0d5c0de77]] and [[Kira Roessler|2c65be73-5658-47c5-9619-01f78db0e2cb]] marry. They later record as the bass duo Dos, and stay friends after the divorce.

years.h: Sometimes, Almost Always fills a gap on SST
years.p: An EP built around Sometimes, a song that later turns up in Santa Cruz skate videos.
Trouser Press called it fIREHOSE's best and most accessible record. It adds country-rock turns like Understanding and Vastopol, and a Hurley drum solo.
years.xp: Trouser Press credited extensive touring for sharpening Crawford's singing. Some tracks lean into conventional '70s country-rock.

years.h: Time with You reaches No. 26 on Billboard's Modern Rock chart
years.p: Crawford's song from fROMOHIO, sent out as an SST promo, gives fIREHOSE its first chart single.

years.h: Skateboarders find fIREHOSE through Santa Cruz videos
years.p: Brave Captain, Sometimes, Hear Me and Windmilling turn up in Santa Cruz Skateboards' Streets on Fire videos, and a skater audience follows.

eras.title: Columbia calls
eras.text: In 1991 the most econo band in America signed with Columbia, and a few fans braced for a sellout. The label got two studio albums and a live EP, and the band ended it themselves in the town where it started.

q: We make records to promote tours.
years.h: fIREHOSE leaves SST for Columbia Records
years.p: The signing surprises fans, some of whom worry about a sellout. Mike Watt's answer, in Encyclopedia.com's account, is that this is how the band has always worked.

years.src: Wikipedia: Flyin' the Flannel · Trouser Press: fIREHOSE
yt: Walking the Cow, Belly Up Tavern, 1993
years.h: Flyin' the Flannel turns Daniel Johnston into a hit
years.p: Produced with Paul Q. Kolderie at Mad Dog in Venice, it's faster and heavier than before. The cover of [[Daniel Johnston|8a7ca8b0-d23c-4eff-8fe9-6220ba5c9c76]]'s Walking the Cow is the surprise success.
years.xp: Trouser Press described the album as bringing back aggressive energy, with a subdued Walking the Cow that did unexpectedly well commercially.

years.h: Live Totem Pole covers Public Enemy, Superchunk and Blue Öyster Cult
years.p: Seven songs recorded at the Palomino in Los Angeles in August 1991.
years.xp: Trouser Press said the set caught the band thriving live, with solid takes on its covers of [[Public Enemy|bf2e15d0-4b77-469e-bfb4-f8414415baca]], [[Superchunk|61653550-fd9b-4401-8248-44f2d064d384]] and [[Blue Öyster Cult|c7423e0c-ab3e-4ab4-be10-cdff5a9d3062]].

years.src: Wikipedia: Mr. Machinery Operator · Trouser Press: fIREHOSE
years.h: J Mascis produces the last fIREHOSE album
years.p: Mr. Machinery Operator is cut at Capitol Studios in Hollywood, with guests [[Nels Cline|afa7b889-c499-4194-9367-7b80c9f88325]], Joe Baiza and [[Mac McCaughan|8841967d-3914-4ab9-aca6-94781aa35288]].
years.xp: Reviews were cool. Entertainment Weekly called it agreeably sedate, Robert Christgau called it a dud, and Trouser Press said it sounded "tired" despite [[J Mascis|82315599-2215-4c3e-a36f-87be58d06ec0]] behind the board.

years.h: About 980 gigs later, the band ends in San Pedro
years.p: The last show is at the Warner Grand Theatre, in Watt and Hurley's hometown, where it started, after seven and a half years.
years.xp: Watt went solo on Columbia with Ball-Hog or Tugboat? in 1995 and later played bass for [[The Stooges|794c6bf2-3241-416f-9b8f-24e2d84a1c4b]]. [[Ed Crawford|c02f03fe-93cf-4590-841b-1b9f04d6a694]] fronted Grand National and toured as a hired guitarist with [[Whiskeytown|fdb40275-50df-4894-8481-573e86956e81]] and [[Southern Culture on the Skids|90c88f94-8b70-49fd-9726-cadf4306ef42]].

eras.title: Smokin' on the ol' pink pole
eras.text: Eighteen years after the Warner Grand, Watt, Hurley and Ed Crawford got back in the van for a two-week run that included both Coachella weekends, with a Columbia anthology out to mark it.

years.cap: Crawford and Watt at the WOW Hall, Eugene, April 10, 2012
years.p: A two-CD anthology of the Columbia albums plus bonus live cuts and instrumentals, out alongside the reunion dates.

years.cap: Crawford, Watt and Hurley at Neumos, Seattle, April 7, 2012
years.p: The 14-date 'Smokin' on the Ol' Pink Pole' tour opens in Sacramento and takes in both weekends of Coachella.
